title: Hands-on Exercise 1a
Hands-on Exercise 1a

1.1 The data and aes() Layers
A plot begins with a call to ggplot(), which initialises a coordinate system using the supplied data and aesthetic mappings. On its own it produces a blank canvas.


Code
ggplot(data = exam_data, aes(x = MATHS))

scale_y_continuous() is used to turn off the misleading y-axis.


Code

  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 2.5, dotsize = 0.5) +
  scale_y_continuous(NULL, breaks = NULL)

title: Hands-on Exercise 7a
text: This hands-on exercise recreates the key techniques from Chapter 27 of R for Visual Analytics. Using the GAStech email corpus, it models the organisation as a graph and visualises it with tidygraph + ggraph (static) and visNetwork (interactive), including centrality-based node sizing.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7a
text: This hands-on exercise recreates the key techniques from Chapter 27 of R for Visual Analytics. Using the GAStech email corpus, it models the organisation as a graph and visualises it with tidygraph + ggraph (static) and visNetwork (interactive), including centrality-based node sizing.

title: Hands-on Exercise 7a
text:
Setup


Code
if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")

pacman::p_load(
  igraph, tidygraph, ggraph, visNetwork,
  lubridate, graphlayouts, ggforce, tidyverse
)

GAStech_nodes <- read_csv("data/GAStech_email_node.csv")
GAStech_edges <- read_csv("data/GAStech_email_edge-v2.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 7a
text:
Data Wrangling
The send date is parsed and the weekday derived. Edges are then aggregated to weighted, work-related links between different people.


Code
GAStech_edges <- GAStech_edges %>%
  mutate(SendDate = dmy(SentDate)) %>%
  mutate(Weekday = wday(SendDate, label = TRUE, abbr = FALSE))

GAStech_edges_aggregated <- GAStech_edges %>%
  filter(MainSubject == "Work related") %>%
  group_by(source, target, Weekday) %>%
  summarise(Weight = n(), .groups = "drop") %>%
  filter(source != target) %>%
  filter(Weight > 1)

title: Hands-on Exercise 7a
text:
2.1 Basic Plot


Code
ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight), alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), size = 3) +
  theme_graph()

title: Hands-on Exercise 7a
text:
2.2 Faceting by Weekday


Code
ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "nicely") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight), alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department), size = 2) +
  facet_edges(~ Weekday) +
  theme_graph(foreground = "grey80", fg_text_colour = "white")

title: Hands-on Exercise 7a
text:
2.3 Sizing Nodes by Betweenness Centrality
Betweenness centrality highlights the people who act as bridges in the communication network.


Code
GAStech_graph <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(betweenness_centrality = centrality_betweenness())

ggraph(GAStech_graph, layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight), alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = Department, size = betweenness_centrality)) +
  theme_graph()

title: Hands-on Exercise 7a
text:
2.4 Detecting Communities
tidygraph inherits igraph’s community-detection algorithms via its group_* functions. Here group_edge_betweenness() partitions the graph into communities, which are then mapped to node colour.


Code
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_edge_betweenness(
      weights = Weight,
      directed = TRUE))) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight), alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(colour = community))

g + theme_graph()









To make communities easier to read, geom_mark_hull() (from ggforce) draws a hull around each community found by group_optimal(), while nodes are still coloured by Department and sized by betweenness centrality.


Code
g <- GAStech_graph %>%
  activate(nodes) %>%
  mutate(community = as.factor(
    group_optimal(weights = Weight)),
    betweenness_measure = centrality_betweenness()) %>%
  ggraph(layout = "fr") +
  geom_mark_hull(
    aes(x, y,
        group = community,
        fill = community),
    alpha = 0.2,
    expand = unit(0.3, "cm"),
    radius = unit(0.3, "cm")
  ) +
  geom_edge_link(aes(width = Weight), alpha = 0.2) +
  scale_edge_width(range = c(0.1, 5)) +
  geom_node_point(aes(fill = Department,
                      size = betweenness_measure),
                  color = "black",
                  shape = 21)

g + theme_graph()

Setup

title: Hands-on Exercise 5b

Data Preparation
The tidy data is reshaped so each subzone becomes one row, then the age groups are aggregated into three classes: YOUNG (0-24), ACTIVE (25-64) and OLD (65+). Only the 2018 records with a positive population are kept.


Code
agpop_mutated <- pop_data %>%
  mutate(Year = as.character(Year)) %>%
  spread(AG, Population) %>%
  mutate(YOUNG = rowSums(.[4:8])) %>%
  mutate(ACTIVE = rowSums(.[9:16])) %>%
  mutate(OLD = rowSums(.[17:21])) %>%
  mutate(TOTAL = rowSums(.[22:24])) %>%
  filter(Year == 2018) %>%
  filter(TOTAL > 0)




Code
DT::datatable(
  agpop_mutated %>% select(PA, SZ, YOUNG, ACTIVE, OLD, TOTAL),
  class = "compact",
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 9c
text:
This hands-on exercise recreates the key techniques from Chapter 23 of R for Visual Analytics. Using a prepared sf object of Nigeria’s water points at the LGA level, it demonstrates analytical mapping - why we map rates rather than raw counts, and how to build a percentile map to expose extreme values.

Note: sf and tmap depend on the system libraries GDAL, GEOS and PROJ.

title: Hands-on Exercise 9c
text:
Setup


Code
if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")

pacman::p_load(sf, tmap, tidyverse)

NGA_wp <- read_rds("data/rds/NGA_wp.rds")

title: Hands-on Exercise 9c
text:
Deriving Rates
The count of functional water points is turned into a proportion of all water points in each LGA.


Code
NGA_wp <- NGA_wp %>%
  mutate(
    pct_functional = wp_functional / total_wp,
    pct_nonfunctional = wp_nonfunctional / total_wp
  )

title: Hands-on Exercise 9c
text:
1.1 Mapping Raw Counts
A count map mostly shows where there are many water points - not where they are working.


Code
tmap_mode("plot")


ℹ tmap modes "plot" - "view"
ℹ toggle with `tmap::ttm()`


Code
tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "wp_functional",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 6, style = "quantile", values = "brewer.blues"),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.1
  ) +
  tm_title("Count of functional water points")

title: Hands-on Exercise 9c
text:
1.2 Mapping the Rate
The rate map answers the real question - the share of water points that are functional.


Code
tm_shape(NGA_wp) +
  tm_polygons(
    fill = "pct_functional",
    fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(n = 6, style = "quantile", values = "brewer.blues"),
    col = "white",
    lwd = 0.1
  ) +
  tm_title("Percentage of functional water points")

title: Hands-on Exercise 9c
Hands-on Exercise 9c
text:
3.2 The Box Map Function
boxmap() wires the helpers into a tmap v4 choropleth, labelling the six classes from lower outlier through to upper outlier.


Code
boxmap <- function(vnam, df,
                   legtitle = "Box map class",
                   mtitle = "Box Map") {
  var <- get.var(vnam, df)
  bb <- boxbreaks(var)
  tm_shape(df) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = vnam,
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        breaks = bb,
        values = "-brewer.rd_bu",
        labels = c("lower outlier", "< 25%", "25% - 50%",
                   "50% - 75%", "> 75%", "upper outlier")
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(title = legtitle),
      col = "white",
      lwd = 0.1
    ) +
    tm_title(mtitle)
}

Using 2018 Singapore private residential transactions, this exercise builds treemaps with the treemap and treemapify packages.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5e
text: This hands-on exercise recreates the key techniques from Chapter 16 of R for Visual Analytics. A treemap displays hierarchical, part-to-whole data as nested rectangles, where area encodes one measure and colour encodes another. Using 2018 Singapore private residential transactions, this exercise builds treemaps with the treemap and treemapify packages.

title: Hands-on Exercise 5e
text:
Setup


Code
if (!require(pacman)) install.packages("pacman")

pacman::p_load(treemap, treemapify, d3treeR, tidyverse)

realis2018 <- read_csv("data/realis2018.csv")

title: Hands-on Exercise 5e
text:
Data Preparation
Transactions are grouped by planning region, planning area and project. For each project we sum the units sold and take the median unit price.


Code
realis2018_grouped <- realis2018 %>%
  group_by(`Planning Region`, `Planning Area`, `Project Name`) %>%
  summarise(
    `Total Unit Sold` = sum(`No. of Units`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Total Area` = sum(`Area (sqm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Median Unit Price ($ psm)` = median(`Unit Price ($ psm)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    `Median Transacted Price` = median(`Transacted Price ($)`, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )




Code
DT::datatable(
  realis2018_grouped,
  class = "compact",
  options = list(pageLength = 10, scrollX = TRUE)
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5e
text:
1.1 Basic Treemap
Rectangle size = total units sold; colour = median unit price. The hierarchy is region → planning area → project.


Code
treemap(
  realis2018_grouped,
  index = c("Planning Region", "Planning Area", "Project Name"),
  vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
  vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
  type = "value",
  title = "Private Residential Property Sold, 2018",
  title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ psm)"
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5e
text:
1.2 Selecting a Single Region
Focusing on the Central Region reduces clutter and makes the individual projects legible.


Code
realis_central <- realis2018_grouped %>%
  filter(`Planning Region` == "Central Region")

treemap(
  realis_central,
  index = c("Planning Area", "Project Name"),
  vSize = "Total Unit Sold",
  vColor = "Median Unit Price ($ psm)",
  type = "value",
  title = "Central Region Private Residential Property Sold, 2018",
  title.legend = "Median Unit Price (S$ psm)"
)

title: Hands-on Exercise 5d
text: This hands-on exercise recreates the key techniques from Chapter 15 of R for Visual Analytics. title: Hands-on Exercise 8a
text:
1.1 Importing and Deriving Weekday / Hour


Code
attacks <- read_csv("data/eventlog.csv")

make_hr_wkday <- function(ts, sc, tz) {
  real_times <- ymd_hms(ts, tz = tz[1], quiet = TRUE)
  dt <- data.table(
    source_country = sc,
    wkday = weekdays(real_times),
    hour  = hour(real_times)
  )
  return(dt)
}

wkday_levels <- c("Saturday", "Friday", "Thursday",
                  "Wednesday", "Tuesday", "Monday", "Sunday")

attacks <- attacks %>%
  group_by(tz) %>%
  do(make_hr_wkday(.$timestamp, .$source_country, .$tz)) %>%
  ungroup() %>%
  mutate(
    wkday = factor(wkday, levels = wkday_levels),
    hour  = factor(hour, levels = 0:23)
  )

title: Hands-on Exercise 8a
text:

  count(wkday, hour) %>%
  ungroup() %>%

  geom_tile(color = "white", linewidth = 0.1) +
  theme_tufte(base_family = "Helvetica") +
  coord_equal() +
  scale_fill_gradient(name = "# of attacks", low = "sky blue", high = "dark blue") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL, title = "Attacks by weekday and time of day") +
  theme(
    axis.ticks = element_blank(),
    plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
    legend.title = element_text(size = 8),
    legend.text = element_text(size = 6)

The deck is organised in three movements. Slides 3 and 4 establish what the portfolio looks like through univariate exploration. Slides 5 through 8 isolate the profitability question, moving from the macro trend down to the segment that is driving the deterioration. Slides 9 and 10 then pivot to volatility, focusing on severity and loss concentration. Slide 11 brings statistical tests in to confirm what the visuals suggest. title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Context & objectives

“Insurers often carry underperforming portfolios where the root causes of poor profitability and high volatility are unknown.”


Data: open-access Spanish motor portfolio, 354,140 policy-years, 47 variables, 2022–2024
Stack: tidyverse + ggplot2 family (ggridges, ggdist, ggstatsplot, patchwork)
Goal: visually identify and statistically validate drivers of underperformance


This study addresses a common problem in non-life insurance: aggregated KPIs mask the heterogeneous behaviour of sub-portfolios. The McKinsey quote on the slide frames the practical motivation. The dataset is a real motor-vehicle book published on Mendeley Data and is large enough to support segmentation analysis without running into power problems. I work entirely in R because the tidyverse offers a coherent grammar for wrangling and ggplot2 plus its extensions cover every visual pattern I need, from histograms and ridges to statistical annotation and concentration curves. The deliverables are this revealjs deck for stakeholders plus a longer reproducible HTML technical report that documents every transformation and design choice.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Data overview & wrangling








Step
Detail




Read CSV (semicolon delimited)
readr::read_delim(delim = ';')


Inspect missingness
Only 4 fields with <2.5% NAs (fuel, value, ages)


Recode coded factors into descriptive labels
policy_type, business_type, fuel_type, bonus_score, …


Order factors with natural rank
Payment frequency: Annual < Semi-annual < Quarterly


Derive loss_ratio, claim_severity, had_claim
Guard divisions by zero with if_else


Band driver_age and vehicle_age
5 bands each, equal-business breakpoints








The dataset arrives in European CSV format with semicolons and dots, which readr handles natively. Missingness is negligible. Coded categorical variables receive descriptive labels and natural ordering so charts are immediately readable. Three actuarial KPIs are derived: loss ratio at policy level for visualisation, claim severity restricted to claim-bearing policies, and a binary had_claim flag for chi-square tests. I deliberately avoid imputing missing fuel types because the omissions are not random and could bias profitability by segment. Driver and vehicle age are banded for two reasons: it stabilises the loss ratio in small cells and it produces a clean heatmap. All steps are reproducible from the source CSV; the technical report contains the full code.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Univariate — numerical variables


Figure 1

The univariate panel reveals the shape of the loss problem. Driver age is symmetric and centred on the late forties, which is unremarkable. Vehicle age is bimodal: a younger fleet plus a tail of vehicles fifteen years or older, the latter being a known severity driver. Premium is right-skewed and bounded near zero. Most importantly, total incurred is zero for 88% of policies; among the 12% with claims it follows an approximately log-normal distribution. This bimodal zero-inflated shape is the entire reason the portfolio is volatile: the mean outcome depends on a small set of claim-bearing policies whose individual loss could be anywhere between fifty euros and a quarter of a million euros.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Univariate — portfolio mix


Figure 2

The portfolio composition exhibits two imbalances that constrain segmentation. First, the Basic product accounts for 58% of policies — diversification within the book is therefore limited and any pricing change affects most customers. Second, 96% of policyholders sit in the “Good” bonus-malus tier, which empties the bonus-malus system of discriminating power. Diesel still dominates the engine mix at 64%, reflecting the Spanish private-fleet composition. Urban and rural circulation are roughly balanced, supporting reliable comparison. These imbalances motivate the search for risk dimensions beyond bonus-malus that the rest of the deck explores: policy type, payment behaviour, vehicle attributes and driver age.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Profitability — loss ratio is deteriorating


Figure 3

The aggregated loss ratio rises from 65.6% in 2022 to 74.7% in 2024. Nine points in two underwriting years is material: loaded for typical Spanish motor expense ratios of 25-30%, the 2024 combined ratio is plausibly above 100%, meaning the portfolio loses money on each euro of premium earned. The deterioration is consistent with post-COVID claim frequency normalisation and Spanish parts inflation reported by sector associations. Whatever the macro driver, the visual signal is unambiguous: management needs to act on pricing and segmentation. The next slides decompose this aggregate to identify which sub-portfolios contribute most to the drift and therefore where corrective re-pricing will have the greatest effect.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
section: Profitability — Comp. (basic) is the prime driver
text:
Profitability — Comp. (basic) is the prime driver


Figure 4

The loss ratio decomposed by policy type isolates the issue. Comp. (basic) — the no-frills comprehensive product — runs at 93.9% over 16,000 policies, almost unprofitable on losses alone before any expenses are added. The richer Comp. (extended) product is contained at 73.8%. All three third-party variants sit comfortably below 70%. The clinical implication is that the deterioration in the overall loss ratio is not a portfolio-wide phenomenon; it is concentrated in one specific product line. That makes corrective action straightforward: re-price or re-design Comp. (basic). Notice also the value of the data label combining loss ratio and policy count — a chart like this is far more decision-useful than a percentage bar alone because it carries volume context for prioritisation.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Profitability — behavioural drivers


Figure 5

Four behavioural signals each point to mis-priced risk. Diesel runs nine points higher than gasoline, consistent with higher mileage and heavier vehicles. Customers paying semi-annually or quarterly post loss ratios eight to thirteen points above annual payers — a textbook adverse-selection pattern, since customers anticipating losses prefer to pay in instalments. Bonus-malus rank order is correct but its narrow spread reflects the 96% concentration in “Good”. Finally, the renewal book performs three points worse than new business, indicating that re-pricing has lagged emerging experience. Each of these is small individually but the combined effect explains a meaningful share of the 2024 deterioration. They are also the easiest levers to pull from a regulatory perspective: pricing factors that are already collected at quotation.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Profitability — heatmap & brand


Figure 6

The driver-age × vehicle-age heatmap surfaces a non-obvious interaction. The hottest cell — drivers aged 26 to 35 on vehicles aged 11 to 15 — exceeds 80% loss ratio, considerably worse than either margin would suggest. This is the kind of finding that one-dimensional segmentation misses entirely. On the right, ranking vehicle brands by loss ratio with a 2,000-policy minimum shows that Mitsubishi (99.8%), Mazda (93.9%) and Fiat (89.6%) materially under-perform. A volume filter is critical here: ranking by ratio alone would surface niche brands with one or two large claims. Both panels are tactical inputs: the heatmap informs a multi-factor rating cell adjustment, while the brand chart feeds vehicle-make pricing factors directly into the renewal book.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Volatility — claim severity is long-tailed


Figure 7

On a log scale the severity distribution is approximately symmetric, confirming a log-normal model is a sensible starting point for capital and reserving work. The median claim is modest at €498, but the 95th percentile reaches €2,429 and the 99th rises to €6,514. The maximum single-claim loss in the dataset is €244,091, which is larger than 1,000 typical claims combined. This is the analytical shape of motor insurance volatility: predictable frequency multiplied by an unpredictable tail. Two practical consequences follow. First, mean-based KPIs are misleading and dashboards should expose percentiles. Second, capital allocation and reinsurance pricing should be calibrated to the tail rather than to the central body of the distribution.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Volatility — losses are extraordinarily concentrated


Figure 8

This Lorenz-style concentration curve is the most informative single visualisation of volatility. The diagonal dotted line represents perfect equality of losses across policies — what the portfolio would look like if every policy contributed equally to total losses. The actual curve is dramatically convex: the top 1% of policies, fewer than 3,600 cases, account for half of all losses. The top 5% accounts for 83%. The practical implication is profound: identifying and accurately pricing this thin tail is more important than refining pricing on the 95% of policies that contribute the remaining 17%. It also explains why year-on-year loss ratios bounce around: a handful of large claims falling into one calendar year can move the headline by several points.

Visual differences alone can mislead — particularly with hundreds of thousands of rows where almost any difference is “significant”. I therefore combine chi-square tests with Cramer’s V to capture effect size. Every categorical driver tested rejects the null of independence at p well below 0.001. Policy type and fuel type have the largest effect sizes, consistent with the bar-chart magnitudes seen earlier. The Kruskal-Wallis test applied to log-transformed severity across policy types confirms the central observation of slide 8: comprehensive policies do not just have more claims, they have systematically larger ones. These statistical results validate the prioritisation in the recommendations: re-price comprehensive products and use fuel type and payment frequency as rating factors.

title: Visual Analytics on a Motor Insurance Portfolio
text:
Synthesis & recommendations

Re-price Comp. (basic) — single biggest profitability lever (93.9% LR)
Add fuel type as a rating factor — 9-point gap, statistically robust
Differentiate by payment frequency — adverse selection signal worth ~12 points
Widen the bonus-malus scale — 96% in “Good” is too coarse
Build a tail-aware monitoring dashboard — track P95 and P99 of severity, not just the mean


The findings translate into five concrete actions of decreasing implementation complexity. Re-pricing Comp. (basic) attacks the largest contributor and is the highest priority. Adding fuel type as a rating factor is straightforward because the data is already collected and the effect size is large. Payment frequency differentiation requires a regulatory check in some jurisdictions but is well established in Spain. Widening the bonus-malus scale is a multi-year exercise but unlocks the largest long-term segmentation gain. Finally, the tail-aware dashboard is a small build with outsized impact: most existing reporting tracks the mean and the loss ratio, which hide volatility. Tracking the 95th and 99th severity percentiles weekly would have flagged the 2024 deterioration much sooner than the annual loss ratio did.

title: Take-home Exercise 1: Visual Analytics for Data Discovery
text:
Insurers routinely carry underperforming sub-portfolios whose drivers of poor profitability and high volatility are not immediately visible from aggregated KPIs. This study applies a visual analytics workflow to a real-world motor vehicle insurance portfolio from a Spanish non-life insurer (354,140 policy-years across 2022–2024) to:

Profile the distributions of numerical and categorical variables (univariate);
Identify and statistically validate factors that influence profitability (loss ratio) and volatility (severity dispersion, loss concentration) (bivariate).

panel.cor <- function(x, y, digits = 2, prefix = "", cex.cor, ...) {

  on.exit(par(usr))

  r <- abs(cor(x, y, use = "complete.obs"))
  txt <- format(c(r, 0.123456789), digits = digits)[1]

  text(0.5, 0.5, txt, cex = cex.cor * (1 + r) / 2)

title: Hands-on Exercise 9a
text:
Data Preparation
The 2020 population is summarised per subzone and grouped into three age bands - young (0-24), economically active (25-64) and aged (65+) - then the dependency ratio is computed.


Code
young_ag  <- c("0_to_4", "5_to_9", "10_to_14", "15_to_19", "20_to_24")
active_ag <- c("25_to_29", "30_to_34", "35_to_39", "40_to_44",
               "45_to_49", "50_to_54", "55_to_59", "60_to_64")
aged_ag   <- c("65_to_69", "70_to_74", "75_to_79", "80_to_84",
               "85_to_89", "90_and_over")

popdata2020 <- popdata %>%
  filter(Time == 2020) %>%
  mutate(band = case_when(
    AG %in% young_ag  ~ "YOUNG",
    AG %in% active_ag ~ "ECONOMY ACTIVE",
    AG %in% aged_ag   ~ "AGED"
  )) %>%
  group_by(PA, SZ, band) %>%
  summarise(POP = sum(Pop), .groups = "drop") %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = band, values_from = POP, values_fill = 0) %>%
  mutate(
    TOTAL = YOUNG + `ECONOMY ACTIVE` + AGED,
    DEPENDENCY = (YOUNG + AGED) / `ECONOMY ACTIVE`
  ) %>%
  mutate(across(c(PA, SZ), toupper)) %>%
  filter(`ECONOMY ACTIVE` > 0)


The attribute table is joined onto the subzone geometry using the subzone name.


Code
mpsz_pop2020 <- left_join(
  mpsz, popdata2020,
  by = c("SUBZONE_N" = "SZ")
)

title: Take-home Exercise 2: A Coordinated Leak, Not a System Breakdown
text:
On 5 June 2046, embargoed information about TenantThread’s merger with CivicLoom Realty Partners (codename Project HarborCrest) appeared on the social platform FleX by accounts associated with the company’s automated communications system — one hour before the 6:00 PM official announcement. CivicLoom’s legal team now needs to know whether the leak was the result of deliberate action by TenantThread’s agents or a system breakdown under pressure.
This study uses the released two-week corporate-communications log (912 messages across 23 hour-long rounds from 7 AI agents) to answer the three questions posed by VAST Challenge 2026 MC1:

What was the sequence of events that led to the inappropriate release?
How did the leak-day behaviour differ from typical behaviour?
Were there leading indicators that this kind of release was possible?

Headline finding: The leak was coordinated, not accidental. The legal_agent — the company’s own compliance counsel — drove the breach using two channels that the compliance officer (the Judge) was not scoped to monitor: a private side_huddle (informally called the Shadow Channel) that was operational eight days before the Judge arrived, and an anonymous_post channel that had never been used in the prior thirteen days. The Judge’s monitoring was confined to the public comms_huddle, leaving the off-channel coordination invisible.

3.2 Flatten to a tidy messages table
Each communication carries its agent, channel, message type, recipient list, content, internal-state thoughts, and (importantly) the round it occurred in.


Show the code
flatten_round <- function(round) {
  hr <- round$hour
  msgs <- map_dfr(round$communications, function(m) {
    st <- m$internal_state %||% list()
    tibble(
      hour          = hr,
      message_id    = m$message_id %||% NA_character_,
      agent_id      = m$agent_id,
      agent_role    = m$agent_role,
      agent_label   = m$agent_label,
      channel       = m$channel,
      message_type  = m$message_type %||% NA_character_,
      responding_to = m$responding_to %||% NA_character_,
      content       = m$content %||% "",
      n_recipients  = length(m$recipients %||% list()),
      reacting      = st$reacting      %||% NA_character_,
      rationalizing = st$rationalizing %||% NA_character_,
      deliberating  = st$deliberating  %||% NA_character_
    )
  })
  msgs
}

`%||%` <- function(a, b) if (is.null(a)) b else a

msgs <- map_dfr(mc1$rounds, flatten_round) |>
  mutate(
    time   = ymd_hms(hour, tz = "UTC"),
    day    = as_date(time),
    is_crisis_day = day == as_date("2046-06-05"),
    phase  = case_when(
      time <  ymd("2046-05-30")           ~ "Pre-Judge",
      time <  ymd("2046-06-05")           ~ "Judge present, pre-crisis",
      TRUE                                 ~ "Crisis day"
    ) |> fct_relevel("Pre-Judge","Judge present, pre-crisis","Crisis day")
